Micro-vortex generators for shock wave/boundary layer interactions
Conical similarity of shock/boundary-layer interactions generated byswept and unswept fins
top_cited_works.abstract: A parametric experimental investigation has been made of the class of three-dimensional shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interactions generated by swept and unswept leading-edge fins. The fin sweepback angles were 0-65 deg at 5, 9, and 15 deg angles of attack. Two equilibrium two-dimensional turbulent boundary layers with a freestream Mach number of 2.95 and a Reynolds number of 6.3 x 10 to the 7th/m were used as incoming flow conditions. All of the resulting interactions were found to possess conical symmetry of the surface flow patterns and pressures outside of an initial inception zone. Further, these interactions were found to obey a simple conical similarity rule based on inviscid shock wave strength, irrespective of fin sweepback or angle of attack. This is one of the first demonstrations of similarity among three-dimensional interactions produced by geometrically dissimilar shock generators.

recent_works.title: Image Processing of Schlieren Images of a Propagating Shock in a Narrow Shock Tube
recent_works.abstract: Schlieren visualization was carried out in a one inch square cross-section shock tube. The shock tube is approximately 1.4 m long, with the 0.3 m long test section attached to the end of the driven section. The shock tube was instrumented with 7 high frequency response PCB transducers to record wall static pressures during experiments. The optical window in the test section is three inches wide and is of the same cross section as the rest of the shock tube. A 4000 lumen, high intensity white light source was collimated into a six inch diameter light beam, which illuminated the test window. High speed videos of the experiments were captured as a sequence of 128 images at 500,000 frames per second with the exposure time being 200 nanoseconds per frame. The images were then post-processed to remove background artifacts and correct for window orientation. Thereafter, the leading edge of the shock wave was detected using Canny algorithm and the shock velocity was calculated using cross-correlation. recent_works.title: Development of Microfabricated Thin Film Gauges for Short Duration Test Facilities
recent_works.abstract: This paper describes the design, modeling, and fabrication of microfabricated thin-film heat-flux gauges (TFGs) for short-duration hypersonic ground-test environments. A onedimensional, transient thermal model of a thin-film–substrate system is formulated and solved using Laplace-transform methods, providing insight into material selection and thickness requirement for fast-response operation. Thermal property matching and coefficient of thermal expansion compatibility are then used to identify suitable film–substrate pairs and guide the overall sensor design. Based on this, thin-film heat-flux gauges are fabricated in-house using standard microfabrication processes used in the semiconductor industry. Static calibration procedures are carried out to characterize the thermophysical response of the sensors. The gauges are currently being prepared for shock tube testing, whereby their heat-flux performance will be evaluated against analytical predictions. Such an integrated modeling-to-fabrication approach presents a robust pathway for developing reliable, fast-response TFGs for hypersonic testing.

recent_works.title: Novel Helium Turbo Compressor for Small Modular Reactor
recent_works.abstract: The helium turbo-compressor is one of the core technologies for a small modular nuclear reactor (SMR), where the helium gas is a primary coolant of the next-generation high-temperature gas reactor. General Atomics Electromagnetic System (GA-EMS) is developing a 100-MW thermal Gas-cooled Fast Reactor (GFR) as a part of the Department of Energy (DOE) ARC-20 program, and the helium turbo-compressor is a part of a power conversion unit coupled to a 44MW permanent magnet generator developed by GA-EMS. The power cycle is a closed-loop Brayton cycle with a recuperator. The design speed of the turbo-compressor is 11,400rpm with a compressor inlet pressure of 3.1MP and pressure ratio of 2.25. The turbine inlet temperature and pressure are 800oC and 7MPa, respectively. This paper presents novel design features of the helium turbo-compressor with very high aerodynamic efficiency and unique mechanical architecture, which incorporates a compact modular design concept with active magnetic bearings (AMBs). recent_works.title: Analytical Study of Matching of Dual Compressor Modules With Turbine for Small Modular Reactors
recent_works.abstract: Abstract An analytical study of a power conversion unit consisting of a dual compressor and a turbine operating on a closed Brayton cycle with helium is presented. The turbomachinery was a constant hub design with two compressor modules and a turbine module. The design code included the capability to perform sweeps of input parameters such as the polytropic efficiency or loss coefficient, degree of reaction, etc. It is required that the pressure rise of each of the two compressor modules be approximately equal. An optimization procedure for the low- and high-pressure compressors resulted in both of them having seven stages. The performance for each of the compressor stages is almost identical. Another optimization procedure for the turbine yielded six stages. Likewise, the performance for each of the turbine stages is almost identical. Performance maps were developed individually for each of the compressor modules and the turbine. Mathematical constraints based on problem physics were used in conjunction with the component maps to trace turbomachinery operating points. recent_works.title: Inverse Method-of-Characteristics Algorithms for Unsteady Gas Flows with Shifting Thermochemical Equilibrium
recent_works.abstract: Method of characteristics (MoC) algorithms were developed to evaluate quasi-one-dimensional, unsteady flows under thermochemical equilibrium. The effect of momentum losses were accounted through a simple, constant friction factor model. Heat losses were evaluated using the Reynolds analogy. For computational efficiency, changes in the gas state thermochemistry were evaluated through curvefits generated using the open-source toolkit Cantera. MoC algorithms developed here employed the inverse marching method and were capable of resolving various gasdynamic phenomena such as weak compression/rarefaction waves, contact surfaces and shock waves. These MoC algorithms were then used to develop reduced-order models representing the gasdynamics of two impulse facilities -- an expansion tube and a detonation-driven shock tube. Expansion tube calculations did not considered losses, so that they could be validated against an equilibrium Riemann solution. The detonation-driven shock tube model focused on the endwall loading in the damping section of an upstream mode detonation tube.
